faqs.question: What is LiteScope AFM used for?
faqs.answer: It's an AFM built to integrate directly inside an SEM chamber, capturing correlated AFM and SEM data on the same sample spot simultaneously, using Correlative Probe and Electron Microscopy (CPEM) technology.

faqs.question: How does CPEM differ from standard correlative microscopy?
faqs.answer: CPEM captures AFM and SEM data at the same time, on the same location, under the same conditions, removing the manual relocation and re-imaging steps standard correlative workflows require.

faqs.question: How long does it take to mount LiteScope in an SEM?
faqs.answer: Under five minutes, thanks to a compact scan head and adaptation plate built for fast SEM integration.

faqs.question: Does LiteScope require laser alignment like standard AFMs?
faqs.answer: No, self-sensing probes eliminate the need for optical detection or laser adjustment entirely.

faqs.question: Can LiteScope work alongside FIB, GIS, or EDX accessories?
faqs.answer: Yes, it's compatible with FIB, GIS, EDX, and other standard SEM accessories.

faqs.question: What material properties can LiteScope measure?
faqs.answer: Mechanical properties like topography, elasticity, and hardness, along with magnetic domain imaging, piezoelectric domain imaging, and electrical properties including conductivity mapping.

faqs.question: Can LiteScope be used as a standalone AFM outside the SEM?
faqs.answer: Yes, it operates as a standalone AFM as well as inside an SEM chamber.

faqs.question: Is the LiteScope controller customizable?
faqs.answer: Yes, the NenoBox control unit is built on an open-hardware DSP controller, allowing customer modifications for non-standard experiments.

longForm.heroHook: AFM and SEM, on the same spot, at the same time. No sample transfer, no lost location.
longForm.heroLead: Correlating AFM and SEM data usually means moving a sample between two instruments and hoping the region of interest survives the trip. LiteScope removes that gap entirely, mounting a full atomic force microscope directly inside your SEM chamber for simultaneous, correlated imaging of the exact same spot. Correlative Probe and Electron Microscopy (CPEM) technology captures AFM and SEM data together, in situ, under identical conditions, then merges them into three-dimensional correlative images. SEM navigation finds the region of interest fast, self-sensing probes skip the laser alignment most AFMs need, and the whole scan head mounts or removes from your SEM in under five minutes.

sections.title: Product Information
sections.description: LiteScope AFM product information: CPEM technology, SEM integration, and multi-property surface characterization.

body.text: LiteScope mounts a complete AFM inside an SEM chamber, capturing AFM and SEM data on the same spot at the same time, under the same conditions, rather than stitching together two separate sessions.

CPEM technology merges topography, material contrast, and mechanical or electrical property data into three-dimensional correlative images, eliminating the repetitive re-locating and re-imaging that separate AFM and SEM sessions normally require.
SEM navigation locates the region of interest first, then guides the AFM tip directly to it, a fast, precise alternative to hunting for a feature blind under an AFM alone.
Self-sensing probes remove the need for optical detection or laser adjustment, a common source of setup time and drift in conventional AFM systems.
The scan head mounts to or removes from most SEM systems in under five minutes, and stays compatible with FIB, GIS, EDX, and other standard SEM accessories.
An open-hardware DSP controller, developed with the Czech Metrology Institute, lets customers modify the system directly rather than working within a closed platform.
LiteScope also runs as a standalone AFM outside the SEM chamber when that's what the work calls for.

body: Traditional correlative microscopy means imaging with one instrument, moving the sample, then trying to relocate the exact same region under a second instrument, a process that eats time and introduces positional error.

CPEM removes both problems at once: AFM and SEM data get captured together, on the same spot, under identical conditions, so there's no relocation step and no guessing whether the two datasets actually line up.

That simultaneous capture extends across a genuinely broad property set: topography, local elasticity, hardness, magnetic domains, piezoelectric domains, conductivity, and surface potential all combine into a single three-dimensional dataset.

items: An AFM that takes hours to integrate into an SEM defeats the purpose of correlative imaging before the first scan even starts. LiteScope's scan head mounts or removes in under five minutes, keeping the SEM available for other work between sessions.
Self-sensing probes are a big part of why that's possible: no optical detection system, no laser to align, no extra setup step standing between mounting the unit and starting a scan.

Once running, LiteScope reaches well beyond basic topography, covering local elastic properties, depth-dependent characterization, magnetic domain imaging, piezoelectric domain imaging, and conductivity mapping, including in insulated areas.
